description: If you made this at the 1M mark, and I see you are approaching the 5M mark right now.... Dude- I\'m a little surprised you lived long enough to get to 5M. I know that the 15A breaker on your home\'s box will protect you, but put up both your hands when it fell over onto you, and having that voltage go across your heart even for milliseconds represents a real risk for arrhythmia. Yes, I know it\'s a small risk, but I would ask you to not roll those dice anymore in this life. I\'m not saying don\'t make great videos or Jacob\'s Ladders- just do those things that we both know you can do to minimize your risks. Mechanical stability counts, I\'m not just talking about electrical safety issues. Good luck and Godspeed, SJG

description: @@DK-sg3oe With a parallel plate capacitor, you can apply any polarity to it. With an electrolytic capacitor, no. Those capacitors are called electrolytic for a reason. Not because they electrolysis during normal operation (that would be a battery), but because electrolysis was used to manufacture them. You see, for a parallel plate capacitor, the thinner the dielectric, the more capacitance you get, so you want a thin dielectric. However, thin dielectrics have troubles adhering to conductor surfaces, so engineers came up with an idea, to grow the dielectric right on the conductor. In a typical aluminum electrolytic capacitor, the dielectric is a thin layer of aluminum oxide grown on top of a piece of aluminum foil. When the capacitor was first manufactured, the foil was rolled up and soaked in the electrolyte and at this moment there are no dielectric yet. Then, they gradually apply voltage on the terminals, which oxides the anode, forming a thin film on it. This process is called forming since forms the dielectric. The higher the forming voltage is, the thicker the dielectric is, thus the less the capacitance but the higher the rated voltage are. When you apply a reverse voltage too fast, the supposed anode becomes the cathode, and electrons flows towards it, thus reducing it back to aluminum. While in the same process the supposed cathode picks up an oxide layer, because the process is too fast, the oxide layer has too much defects making it not insulating. Now you have a capacitor with no dielectric, so you are essentially boiling water in it with resistive heating. A bang is thus inevitable.
